extracted.intended_audience: architects, architectural students, and designers concerned with Gothic/tracery/window and aperture detailing
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and aesthetic guidelines for designing and protecting window tracery, glazing placement, aperture roofs/porches, and rules for superimposing stories and shafts in buildings, with attention to structural support, light admission, and expressive effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support bars spaced at proper intervals
rubrics_metrics.description: Window bars (mullions) should be supported at proper intervals; however high the window, it is almost impossible that it should require more than two cross bars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use at most two cross bars in general; ensure bars have intermediate support so they do not buckle or allow masonry settlement to distort arches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thicken cross bars to bond close windows
rubrics_metrics.description: When tall windows are placed very close together the masonry between them may need additional support; cross bars of the windows may then be thickened to bond the intermediate piers more strongly together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the increased thickness appears ungainly, modify it by decoration rather than weakening the structural intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame window bars together for mutual support
rubrics_metrics.description: Connect the window bars among themselves so as to frame them together and give the utmost possible degree of support to the whole window head in case of settlement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not merely let bar ends into the voussoirs of the heading; instead join bars by small arches between smaller bars, large arches between larger bars, a comprehensive arch over the whole, or a horizontal lintel for flat-headed windows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pierced spandrils to admit light
rubrics_metrics.description: Spandrils of the arch-supporting system should be light and let as much light through as possible; pierce them (e.g., with circles) to form traceries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small circles + strong stonework produce traceries like Giotto and the Pisan school; larger circles + slender bars yield the Northern Gothic traceries. Choose piercing according to stone strength and desired light admission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tracery variety determined by size, arch height, and head relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Varieties of tracery design arise from the size of the window (number of bars), heights of pointed arches, and the position of the window head relative to the roof, as well as aesthetic/expressional requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within limits, some structural strength may be gracefully sacrificed to achieve variety in traceries; the pointed arch allows more variety than the round arch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circular (wheel) window form
rubrics_metrics.description: In circular windows, vertical bars cannot have secure footing or heading; a small central circle is used to give footing to radiating bars, which are arranged as spokes and properly capitaled and arch-headed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This spoke arrangement (wheel window) is the best tracery form for circular openings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tracery forms derived from gravity and cohesion (timeless forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfect forms of Gothic tracery arrive from laws of gravity and cohesion, not from arbitrary authority or school; they are 'eternal forms' tied to structural laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designs that respect these material and structural laws are likely to be fundamentally sound and enduring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use thicker/massy shafts where glazing not required
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases like triforium and cloister lights where glazing is not required, bars (shafts) may have a more important function—giving steadiness, tone, protection, or seclusion—and thus may be much thicker with massy arches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such heavier traceries often resolve into true colonnades with paired/triple/quadruple arches and small rosettes above them; use the heavier form where appropriate rather than forcing glazed tracery everywhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow functionally-appropriate aesthetic indulgence
rubrics_metrics.description: Because traceries are ordinarily stronger than absolutely necessary, a portion of strength may be 'gracefully sacrificed' to achieve variety within certain limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sacrifice some structural reserve only where safe, to attain aesthetic variety—but remain aware of limits set by structure and material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affectations and degenerate schools (Flamboyant, German, Perpendicular)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be wary of stylistic affectations that depart from perfect forms: Flamboyant (excessive fantasy/effeminacy), German intersectional (cuts continuous features, sacrifices foundation/continuity), and English Perpendicular (aggregates weak arrangements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the historical faults: do not turn subordinated bars into equal ones, do not multiply cross bars unnecessarily, and avoid practices that expose the structure to apparent dislocation or that remove necessary capitals/bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain subordination of bars (avoid equalizing all mullions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfect tracery uses subordinated bars (less to greater). Making a group of bars all exactly equal (creating equal spaces) is a fault (as in English Perpendicular).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve hierarchical sizing of mullions to express structural logic and avoid monotonous or weak-looking composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not run vertical bars into the arch head unchecked
rubrics_metrics.description: Vertical bars should not be simply let into the arch head (voussoirs), because masonry settlement would distort the arch or break/push the bars; instead bars must be framed so they give mutual support to the head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a bar receives an arch heading, treat it as a shaft (capitall it) and connect with arches/lintels so settlement loads are shared.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a bar receives an arch heading, capital it
rubrics_metrics.description: The moment a bar receives an arch heading it is to be treated as a shaft and capitalled (given a capital and base).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not leave bars with arch headings without proper shaft treatment; capitals/bases express the role and help structurally and visually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section of main tracery bars: thickness in depth not breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: For admitting as much light as possible, the bar's thickness should be chiefly in the depth of the window; increasing depth allows diminishing breadth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ double groups of shafts set edgeways, adding a central member into which the glass is fitted and a curved recess behind the shafts—this yields the 'perfect' section for main tracery bars in good Gothic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triforium/cloister tracery sections omit central glass member
rubrics_metrics.description: In triforium and cloister tracery, which has no glass to hold, the central member is omitted and the pure double shaft or a single more massy shaft is used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose pure double shaft for grace; use single massy shaft for simplicity and common practice where glazing is not required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic (Venetian) traceries: shafts as structural supports with glazing behind
rubrics_metrics.description: In Venetian domestic traceries shafts become main vertical supports of floors/walls and are therefore very thick; glazing is thrown behind the pillars and attached to their abaci and bases with iron.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This preserves the symmetry and shade of the shafts while allowing free egress (doors into balconies). Attach glazing to pillar capitals/bases rather than driving fittings into the shafts themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glass position (depth) affects light and viewing convenience
rubrics_metrics.description: When glass position is not fixed, the deeper the glass is set (within given wall thickness), the more light enters and the clearer the prospect from the centre of a room; the farther out the glass is set, the more convenient it is for a person rising and looking out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose deeper setting for occupants who remain at rest and value inward light; choose outward setting where looking out is expected. Consider trade-offs: increased light vs loss of space and colder interior air, and exterior recessed protection from glare and rain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aperture protection: channel jambs and/or add small roof
rubrics_metrics.description: Protect delicate or valuable aperture fillings (colored glass, tracery, sculpture) from rain by channelling the jambs and arch head (aperture mouldings) and, where necessary, by adding external roofing (dripstone moulding) conceived as a small roof projecting from the wall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mouldings alone are often decorative and insufficient as rain channels; an external projecting form (gable, dripstone, or small roof) gives better protection except for rain beating into the aperture area itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a gable as the proper form for aperture projection
rubrics_metrics.description: A deep gable is best for throwing off rain; even a low gable is better than a high arch. Flat roofs should be used only when a gable would be unsightly or when shade rather than rain protection is the object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gable projections can be unsupported, carried on brackets/spurs, or borne on walls/shafts; select the support mode appropriate to scale and safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bracketed/spurred gable projection is a universal good type
rubrics_metrics.description: Gabled dripstones carried on small brackets or spurs form a beautiful and natural type found across all good architecture (from cottages to high architecture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form is easy in wood construction and can be scaled up in stone with slabs or a sub-arch where jointed masonry is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Porch form (walls/shafts carrying projection) is the perfect aperture protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Substituting walls or pillars for brackets allows projecting as far out as desired and forms the perfect porch—adaptable from cottage porches to cathedral porches (when properly modified with arches/pinnacles where necessary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arch spans become large, provide sub-arches, suitable shaft forms and pinnacles where needed to resist lateral thrust; this is the best type of aperture protection historically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unite adjacent porches to avoid embayed intervals
rubrics_metrics.description: When porches carried by walls are placed close together, leave their walls open wider or close intermediate intervals so that damp does not lodge and people are not 'embayed' in uncomfortable recesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unite porches into one range of open caverns to direct crowds and meet lateral thrusts; remove pinnacles where arches meet and install waterspouts between arches to manage drainage (as in great northern porches like Rheims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer rational pediment+sill+shafts over useless horizontal cornices
rubrics_metrics.description: Renaissance pedimental treatments often produce deep dark triangular cavities that hide ornament and do not protect window heads well; a complete pediment with shafts or pilasters on a bracketed sill is a more rational and sometimes beautiful alternative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where Renaissance forms are well designed (e.g., some Whitehall examples), they can be effective; still, ensure pedimental composition serves protection and proportion rather than merely hiding ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superimposition only when necessary for proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not divide a building into stories (superimpose tiers) unless the building's proportions are too large to be justly measured by the eye; divisions should mark bulk and may increase unity if done decoratively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer one grand mass where possible; divide into stories to signal height/proportion rather than as gratuitous ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two correct kinds of superimposition: weight on lightness and lightness on weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Wisely practised superimposition is of two kinds—weight on lightness (e.g., inhabited parts elevated above arcades) or lightness on weight (e.g., light elements over massive base); superimposing weight on weight or lightness on lightness is nearly always wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure support is adequate to the imposed loads and that visual expression matches structural logic; avoid stacking similar qualities that produce awkward or unstable-looking compositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make support visibly adequate (do not conceal necessary structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Passive architecture that appears to lack sufficient visible support is painful to the eye; concealing necessary ironwork or making heavy loads appear carried on insufficient elements creates discomfort and sense of insecurity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express structural supports honestly, or ensure that concealed supports are convincing in proportion; do not create apparent contradictions such as large stone above thin concealed rods of iron.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use superimposition to raise inhabited parts above damp ground
rubrics_metrics.description: Superimposition is often necessary to elevate inhabited parts above ground level in damp/inundated areas; ground stories may be left open as arcades while upper apartments are raised on pillars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This strategy produces picturesque street effects and practical solutions in warm countries and in places like Venice; where ground becomes valuable, ground floors may be enclosed later but the structural logic remains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shaft proportions: keep shafts short relative to wall height above
rubrics_metrics.description: In proportion to the height of wall above them, shafts are to be short; you may turn portions of wall into shaft, but you must not convert all into tall shafts and then add more wall above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shorter shafts must be proportionately thicker; adjust shaft length and diameter together to preserve sensible proportions (e.g., in the Ducal Palace the shortest shafts are the thickest).
